
▸ Thought for 7s

  TCP congestion control is a set of mechanisms designed to prevent a sender
  from overwhelming the network with more data than intermediate routers and
  links can handle. Because the internet is a shared, decentralized system
  with no central traffic controller, each TCP sender must infer network
  conditions on its own. It does this primarily by maintaining a variable
  called the congestion window, which limits the amount of unacknowledged
  data that can be in flight at any given time. The sender continuously
  adjusts this window in response to feedback from the network, such as
  acknowledgments arriving on time or packets being dropped.

  When a new connection begins, TCP starts in a phase called slow start.
  Rather than immediately blasting data at full speed, the sender begins with
  a small congestion window and doubles it every round-trip time as
  acknowledgments return. This exponential growth allows the connection to
  quickly discover available bandwidth without causing immediate congestion.
